readings.c1s1:
¶
'''Turko,''' ''n.'' See ''Turco''<sup>1</sup>.

'''turkois,''' ''n.'' See ''turquoise.''

'''Turkoman''' (tėr′kō-mạn), ''n.'' [Also ''Turcoman;'' = F. ''Turcoman, Turkoman'' = G. ''Turkomane'' (Russ. ''Turkmenetsŭ,'' etc.); ult. < Pers. Turk. ''Turk,'' Turk.] A member of a branch of the Turkish race, found chiefly in central Asia (in Russian territory), Persia, and Afghanistan. {{smaller|Nearly all are nomads. Among the tribes are the Tekkes of Merv and Akhal, the Sariks, etc. Also ''Turkman.''—'''Turkoman carpet,''' a carpet made by the nomads on the northern frontiers of Persia, usually simple in design, but of soft and long nap and rich colors.}}

'''Turk’s-cap''' (tėrks′kap), ''n.'' '''1.''' The martagon-lily, ''Lilium Martagon;'' also, the American swamp-lily, ''L. superbum.'' Also called ''Turk’s-cap lily.'' See ''martagon'' and ''lily.''—'''2.''' A species of melon-cactus, ''Melocactus communis.'' Also ''Turk’s-cap cactus, Turk’s-head.''—'''3.''' A variety of winter squash.

'''Turk’s-head''' (tėrks′hed), ''n.'' '''1.''' Same as ''Turk’s-cap,'' 2.—'''2.''' ''Naut.,'' a form of knot made by weaving turns of small cord round a larger rope. A similar knot is largely used in ornamenting whip-handles.—
[[FIGURE]]
{{c|{{smaller|Turk’s-head, 2.}}}}
'''3.''' A long broom with spherical head, for sweeping ceilings, etc.
{{smaller block|He saw a great ''Turk’s-head'' besom poked up at him.
{{right|''Bulwer,'' My Novel, x. 20.}}}}
'''4.''' A pan for baking cake, having a tin core in the center, thus bringing heat into the middle of the cake.
readings.c1s2:
¶
'''Turk’s-turban''' (tėrks′tėr″ba̤n), ''n.'' A plant of the genus ''Ranunculus''; crowfoot.

'''turky<sup>1</sup>†''', ''n.'' An obsolete spelling of ''turkey''.

'''turky<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' [Abbr. of ''Turky-stone'', ''Turkey-stone''.] Same as ''Turkey-stone'', 1. ''Sandys'', Travailes, p. 173.

'''Turky-stone†''', ''n.'' See ''Turkey-stone''.

'''Turky-wheat†''', ''n.'' See ''Turkey-wheat''.

'''Turlington’s balsam.''' See ''benzoin''.

'''turlough''' (tėr′loċh), ''n.'' [< Ir. ''turloch'', a dry lake, < ''tur'', bare, dry, + ''loch'', lake: see ''lough''.] In Ireland, a temporary pond or lake in certain limestone districts.
{{smaller block|Some [sluggas] are abrupt deep holes, others open into shallow hollows; and when the water during floods rises in the latter, it overflows the adjoining lands, forming the ''turloughs'', which are usually lakes in winter and callows in summer.
{{right|''Kinahan'', Geol. of Ireland, p. 325.}}}}

'''Turlupin''' (tėr′lū-pin), ''n.'' [OF., appar. a particular use, in contempt, of ''turlupin'', “a grub, mushrome, start-up, new-nothing man of no value” (Cotgrave, ed. 1611); origin unknown.] In ''eccles. hist.'', a name given to the members of a French sect of about the fourteenth century, which held views very similar to those of the Brethren of the Free Spirit.
readings.c1s3:
¶
{{smaller block|The ''Turlupins'' were first known by the names Beghards, or Beghins, and brothers and sisters of the free spirit. The common people alone called them ''Turlupins'', a name which seems obviously to be connected with the wolvish howlings which these people, in all probability, would make in their religious ravings. Their subsequent name of the fraternity of poor men might have been the cause why the wandering rogues, called Bedlam beggars, assumed or obtained the title of ''Turlupins'' or Turlygoods, especially if their mode of asking alms was accompanied by the gesticulations of madmen.
{{right|''Douce'', Ill. of Shakspeare.}}}}

'''turm''' (tėrm), ''n.'' [< L. ''turma'', a troop; cf. ''turba'', a troop, crowd: see ''turba'', ''turbid''.] A troop; a turma.
{{smaller block|Legions and cohorts, ''turms'' of horse and wings.
{{right|''Milton'', P. R., iv. 66.}}}}

'''turma''' (tėr′mä), ''n.''; pl. ''turmæ'' (-mē). [L.: see ''turm''.] Among the Romans, a company of cavalry, consisting at first of thirty and afterward of thirty-two men.

'''turmalin, turmaline''' (tėr′ma̤-lin), ''n.'' Same as ''tourmalin''.

'''turmeric''' (tėr′me-rik), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''turmerick'' (NL. ''turmerica'', Minsheu); cf. F. ''terre-mé-''

The rhizome of ''Curcuma longa'', a plant of the ginger family, native and long cultivated in the East Indies. {{smaller|It has a central ovoid body and lateral elongated tubers, called respectively ''round'' and ''long turmeric'', formerly supposed to come from different species. {{smaller block|The ''Turlupins'' were first known by the names Beghards, or Beghins, and brothers and sisters of the free spirit. The common people alone called them ''Turlupins'', a name which seems obviously to be connected with the wolvish howlings which these people, in all probability, would make in their religious ravings. {{smaller block|Legions and cohorts, ''turms'' of horse and wings.

'''turmeric''' (tėr′me-rik), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''turmerick'' (NL. ''turmerica'', Minsheu); cf. F. ''terre-mérite'' (NL. ''terra merita''), turmeric (as if < L. ''terra'', earth, + ''merita'', deserved, deserving, taken in the forced sense of ‘excellent’); both prob. corruptions of an Oriental name, perhaps of Ar. ''kurkum'', saffron: see ''curcuma''.] '''1.''' The rhizome of ''Curcuma longa'', a plant of the ginger family, native and long cultivated in the East Indies. {{smaller|It has a central ovoid body and lateral elongated tubers, called respectively ''round'' and ''long turmeric'', formerly supposed to come from different species. Turmeric is of a deep brownish or greenish yellow, inwardly orange, of a resinous consistence and peculiar aromatic odor. It is prepared for use by grinding. In India it is most largely employed as a condiment, particularly as an ingredient in curry-powders. It has the property of an aromatic stimulant, and is there given internally for various troubles, and applied externally for skin-diseases. In western countries its chief use (now declining) has been that of a dyestuff, in which capacity it affords beautiful but fugitive shades of yellow; at present a leading use is in the preparation of a test-paper called ''turmeric-paper'' or ''curcuma-paper.'' The coloring matter is called ''curcumin;'' and the oil to which its aromatic taste and smell are due, ''turmeric-oil'' or ''turmerol.'' Sometimes called ''Indian saffron.'' The Hindu name is ''huldee.''}} '''2.''' The plant producing turmeric.—'''3.''' The bloodroot, ''Sanguinaria Canadensis.''—{{smaller|'''African turmeric,''' the rootstock of a species of ''Canna,'' having properties like those of turmeric, cultivated in Sierra Leone, and much used by the natives for dyeing yellow.}}

'''turmeric-paper''' (tėr′mẹ-rik-pā″pėr), ''n.'' See ''paper.''

'''turmeric-plant''' (tėr′mẹ-rik-plant), ''n.'' Same as ''turmeric'', 2.

'''turmeric-tree''' (tėr′me-rik-trē), ''n.'' A rutaceous tree, ''Acronychia Baueri,'' of southeastern Australia. {{smaller|It is a moderate-sized tree with a hard, close-grained, and strong yellow wood, and a bright-yellow inner bark used for dyeing.}}

'''turmerol''' (tėr′mẹ-rol), ''n.'' [< ''turmer''(''ic'') + ''-ol.''] Turmeric-oil.

'''turmoil''' (tėr′moil), ''v.'' [Formerly also ''turmoyle;'' prob. from an OF. verb connected with OF. ''tremouille,'' also ''trameul,'' also ''tremoie, tremuye, tremie,'' the hopper of a mill, < ''tremuer,'' agitate, < L. ''tremere,'' shake, tremble: see ''tremble.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To disturb; agitate; trouble; disquiet.
<poem>A ship vnto a certaine haven bent,
''Turmoilde'' in Neptunes watry element.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Times’ Whistle'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 143.}}}}

{{smaller block|In his time Island was ''turmoiled'' with many fierce mutinies.
{{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', I. 571.}}}}

{{smaller block|Quentin resorted to a solitary walk, . . . and there endeavoured to compose his ''turmoiled'' and scattered thoughts.
{{right|''Scott'', Quentin Durward, v.}}}}

'''II.†''' ''intrans.'' To labor amid trouble, worriment, or vexation; be disquieted or in trouble; worry.

{{smaller block|I was once in examination before five or six bishops, where I had much ''turmoiling''.
{{right|''Latimer'', Misc. Sel.}}}}

{{smaller block|Some notable Sophister lies sweating and ''turmoyling'' under the inevitable and mercilesse dilemma’s of Socrates.
{{right|''Milton'', Apology for Smectymnuus.}}}}

'''turmoil''' (tėr′moil), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''turmoyle''; < ''turmoil'', ''v.''] Distracting stir, bustle, commotion, confusion, or din; tumult; disturbance; agitation; trouble; disquiet.

<poem>There I’ll rest, as after much ''turmoil''
A blessed soul doth in Elysium.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., ii. 7. 37.}}}}

='''Syn.''' Confusion, bustle, uproar.

'''turmoilous†''', ''a.'' [Early mod. E. ''termoylous''; < ''turmoil'' + ''-ous''.] Troublous.

{{smaller block|Saynct Augustyne . . . was surelye an excellente man, of dyuyne witte, and knowledge, and so trauayled in settynge foorth Christes true Relygion in those ''termoylous'' dayes . . . that he is worthelye called a Doctour and Pyller of Christes Churche.
{{right|''R. Eden'', First Books on America (ed. Arber), p. 10.}}}}

'''turn''' (tėrn), ''v.'' [Early mod. E. also ''tourn'', ''torn''; < ME. ''turnen'', ''tyrnen'', ''tirnen'' (< AS.), also ''tournen'', ''tornen'' (< OF.); AS. ''tyrnan'', ''turnian'', turn (cf. G. ''turnen'', tilt, just, practise gymnastics, also MHG. G. ''turnieren'', tilt, just, tourney, = Icel. ''turna'', turn, ''turnera'', tilt, tourney, < OF.), = OF. ''torner'', ''tourner'', F. ''tourner'' = Pr. Sp. Pg. ''tornar'' = It. ''tornare'', < L. ''tornare'', turn in a lathe, round off, ML. turn (in various uses) (cf. Gr. τορνεύειν, work with a turners’ chisel, turn in a lathe, round off, turn, τορνοῦσθαι, make round), < ''tornus'', < Gr. τόρνος, a tool used by carpenters to draw circles with, a kind of compasses, also a turners’ chisel; akin to τορός, piercing, < τείρειν, pierce, L. ''terere'', rub away: see ''terebrate'', ''trite'', ''try''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To form or fashion (a piece of wood or metal), with a chisel, while the object is rotated in a lathe; shape, as wood, metal, or other hard substance, especially into round or rounded figures, by means of a lathe: as, to ''turn'' the legs of a chair or a table; to ''turn'' ivory figures.
{{smaller block|A ''turnid'' beddstedd corded x<sup>s</sup>.
{{right|Quoted in ''H. Hall’s'' Society in Elizabethan Age, App., I.}}
I could ''turn'' you a rare handle for that crutch-stick.
{{right|''Dickens'', Our Mutual Friend, iv. 16.}}}}

'''2.''' To round; execute in rounded outlines; bring to perfection of shape, form, or style; hence, to form, fashion, or shape in any way: as, to ''turn'' a sentence.
{{smaller block|The edge . . . is decked with many pretty litle ''turned'' pillers, either of marble or free stone, to leane over.
{{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 205.}} Bring all to the forge and file again; ''torn'' it anew.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Discoveries.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>To play with this smooth, round,
And well-''torned'' chin, as with the billiard ball.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Devil is an Ass, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>But now, my muse, a softer strain rehearse,
''Turn'' every line with art, and smooth thy verse.</poem>
{{right|''Addison'', The Greatest English Poets.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Then her shape
From forehead down to foot perfect—again
From foot to forehead exquisitely ''turn’d.''</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Lancelot and Elaine.}}}}
'''3.''' To adapt; make suitable, fit, or proper.
{{smaller block|However improper he might have been for studies of a higher nature, he was perfectly well ''turned'' for the occupations of trade and commerce.
{{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 108.}}}}
{{smaller block|A man who is not ''turned'' for mirthful meetings of men, or assemblies of the fair sex. ''Steele'', Spectator, No. 49.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>My self not trying, or not ''turn’d'' to please,
May lay the Line, and measure out the Ways.</poem>
{{right|''Congreve'', Of Pleasing.}}}}
'''4.''' To cause to revolve about an axis, or to move round on or as on a center; cause to rotate: as, to ''turn'' a crank.
{{smaller block|She would have made Hercules have ''turned'' spit.
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, ii. 1. 261.}}}}
'''5.''' To execute by whirling or revolving.
{{smaller block|Here is a boy that loves to run, swim, kick football, ''turn'' somersets. ''O. W. Holmes'', Professor, viii.}}
'''6.''' To revolve in the mind; regard from different points of view; consider and reconsider; ponder.
{{smaller block|''Turn'' these ideas about in your mind, and take a view of them on all sides. ''Watts.''}} '''7.''' To go, pass, or move round; go or get round or to the other side of: as, to ''turn'' the stake-boat in a race.
{{smaller block|My tutor appears so able that . . . it must be my own fault if I am not a complete rogue before I ''turn'' the corner.
{{right|''Sheridan'', School for Scandal, iii. 1.}}}}
'''8.''' To change the course or direction of; cause to move, tend, or be aimed or pointed in an opposite or different direction, or toward a different object, purpose, or the like; divert from one way, course, or channel into another.
{{smaller block|He’ll ''turn'' your current in a ditch. {{right|''Shak.'', Cor., iii. 1. 96.}}}}
{{smaller block|He had very much ''turned'' his studies . . . into the lives of Don Bellianis of Greece, Guy of Warwick, “the Seven Champions,” and other historians of that age.
{{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 95.}}}}
{{smaller block|The king now ''turned'' his thoughts upon a nobler object.
{{right|''Bruce'', Source of the Nile, II. 72.}}}}
{{smaller block|The king, who would never have made such a devise in his better days, was more easily ''turned'' from his purpose now than he would once have been.
{{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., ii. 24.}}}}
{{smaller|Hence—(''a'') To head off: as, to ''turn'' a runaway horse. (''b'') To reverse; repeal.}}
{{smaller block|God will ''turn'' thy captivity, and have compassion upon thee. {{right|Deut. xxx. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|It is not in thy power to ''turn'' this destiny.
{{right|''Fletcher (and another ?)'', Prophetess, iii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller|(''c'') To direct; aim: as, to ''turn'' the hose on a burning building.}}
{{smaller block|A man, though he ''turns'' his eyes toward an object, yet he may choose whether he will curiously survey it. {{right|''Locke.''}}}}
{{smaller block|As he gazed with wonder, the youth ''turned'' upon him a piece of lighted bog-wood which he carried in a lantern.
{{right|''Scott'', Fair Maid of Perth, xxix.}}}}
{{smaller|(''d'') To put or apply; use or employ; utilize: as, to ''turn'' everything to advantage or account. <poem>
Great Apollo
''Turn'' all to the best!</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., iii. 1. 15.}}}}
{{smaller block|I am a man out of all business, and would willingly ''turn'' my head to any thing for an honest livelihood.
{{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 251.}}}}
{{smaller block|Some, who ''turn'' their travels to the greatest advantage, endeavour to mix with the people of the country, and with all strangers, in order to make proper observations on customs and manners.
{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. ii. 277.}}}}
{{smaller|(''e'') To blunt (literally by turning over): as, to ''turn'' the edge of a knife. See the phrase below. (''f'') To send; drive; force: with ''off, out, upon'', etc.: as, to ''turn'' cattle ''out'' to feed; to ''turn'' a servant ''out'' of the house.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>
And ȝif thei talke of tales vn-trewe,
Thou ''torn'' hem ''out'' of that entent.</poem>
{{right|''Hymns to Virgin'', etc. (E. E. T. S.), p. 108.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>
Let me be corrected,
To break my stubbornness, if it be so,
Rather than ''turn'' me ''off''; and I shall mend.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Philaster, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|A vessel sent by some merchants to carry provisions to La Tour was fallen into the hands of D’Aulnay, who had made prize of her, and ''turned'' the men ''upon'' an island.
{{right|''Winthrop'', Hist. New England, II. 267.}}}}
'''9.''' To change the position of; shift or change to or as to the top, bottom, front, or back; reverse or invert; turn upside down or inside out: as, to ''turn'' an hour-glass; to ''turn'' flapjacks on a griddle; to ''turn'' one’s coat.
{{smaller block|If I were angry, I might ''turn'' the Buckle of my Girdle behinde me.
{{right|''S. Alexsander'', quoted in Winwood’s Memorials, i. 453.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
